      "content": "## 1. Introduction

[Swap](https://www.baeldung.com/linux/swap-space) is a [virtual memory subsystem](https://www.baeldung.com/cs/virtual-memory-vs-swap-space) mechanism for allocating and maintaining a special part of [secondary storage](https://www.baeldung.com/linux/cli-hardware-info#secondary-storage-disk) as [swap space](https://www.baeldung.com/cs/virtual-memory-vs-swap-space#introduction-to-swap-space). Swap space acts similarly to a main memory (RAM) extension. In short, the kernel moves or swaps out chunks of data called pages from RAM to secondary storage when not in use for a long time and swaps them back in when requested, resulting in a kind of cache. While [swap can be a partition or file](https://www.baeldung.com/linux/swap-file-partition), its main setting is the so-called [swappiness](https://www.baeldung.com/linux/file-system-caching#2-configuring-swappiness).

In this tutorial, **we’ll talk about swappiness and its current default value in the Linux kernel**. First, we go over the general swap strategy of the Linux kernel. After that, we turn to swappiness, what it means, and how to set it. Finally, we explore steps to test the performance of the swappiness setting for a given system.

We tested the code in this tutorial on Debian 11 (Bullseye) with GNU Bash 5.1.4. It should work in most POSIX-compliant environments unless otherwise specified.

## 2. Swap Strategy

In general, **we can split page types into two**:

- filesystem pages in the file cache – program contents, program data, shared libraries, and similar
- anonymous pages in anonymous memory – dynamic runtime data like program stack and heap, as well as [*mmap()*](https://www.baeldung.com/linux/memory-mapped-file-vs-anonymous-memory) allocations

Since it’s already on secondary storage, the filesystem page type doesn’t require swap space. Conversely, anonymous pages are part of volatile memory, so swapping is necessary to preserve this type in certain cases:

```
+-------------------+           +------------------------------+
| Main Memory (RAM) | Swap Out  | Secondary Storage (HDD, SSD) |
+-------------------+ >>>>>>>>> +------------------------------+
| FP1, FP2, ... FPn |  (SLRU)   | Swap | AP - Anonymous Pages  |
| AP1, AP2, ... APn |           |------------------------------|
|                   |  Swap In  | FP - Filesystem-backed Pages |
+-------------------+ <<<<<<<<< +------------------------------+
```
Although it isn’t mandatory, **having swap increases the choices the kernel has for freeing RAM**. Without the feature, we can only free main memory from filesystem-backed pages. On the other hand, having swap space doesn’t mean it will be used.

Still, when there is no swap space, the Linux kernel may need to overcommit memory. In these cases, there is a higher chance of running out of physical memory and having no ability to swap to secondary storage. As a result, the [out-of-memory-killer (OOM-killer) mechanism](https://www.baeldung.com/linux/memory-overcommitment-oom-killer) kicks in and kills rogue processes.

Thus, it’s often good to have even a small amount of swap and reduce swapping rather than none at all.

## 3. Swappiness

According to the official [kernel virtual memory subsystem documentation](https://www.kernel.org/doc/Documentation/sysctl/vm.txt), **the swappiness setting is a value between 0-200 that determines how often the kernel swaps memory pages**:

- high swappiness = more frequent swaps
- low swappiness = less frequent swaps

In other words, the setting decides whether the kernel will swap out more filesystem-backed (lower swappiness) or more anonymous (higher swappiness) pages. So, configuring the minimum swappiness of 0 means the kernel would wait until it has no choice but to swap, which may result in [thrashing](https://www.baeldung.com/cs/virtual-memory-thrashing) or the aforementioned OOM-killer activation. The maximum swappiness value is 200.

### 3.1. Swappiness Settings

Apart from the swap statistics in */proc/meminfo*, like [huge pages](https://www.baeldung.com/linux/huge-pages-management) and others, we can check and set a number of general configuration options in */proc*.

For instance, ***/proc/sys/vm/swappiness* shows us the current swappiness value**:

```
$ cat /proc/sys/vm/swappiness
60
```
Here, we see the default swappiness value of *60*.

Of course, **we can change the swappiness setting directly in the *swappiness* file or via [*sysctl*](https://www.baeldung.com/linux/ipv6-disable#the-proc-pseudo-filesystem-and-the-sysctl-tool)**:

```
$ sysctl vm.swappiness=10
vm.swappiness = 10
```
In this case, we changed the swappiness to *10*.

### 3.2. Filesystem-Backed and Anonymous Page Priority

In the context of swap, **anonymous page priority coincides with the default swappiness of 60, while file-cached pages have a default priority of 200 minus the swappiness value**:

```
+------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Swappiness | Anonymous Page Priority | File-Cached Page Priority |
|------------+-------------------------+---------------------------|
|     60     | = Swappiness = 60       | = 200 - Swappiness = 140  |
+------------------------------------------------------------------+
```
This means both priorities added together make up the maximum value of swappiness *200,* with anonymous pages getting swapped less often by default.

Thus, *vm.swappiness = 100* makes both page type priorities equal, adequate for systems with a high amount of secondary storage usage. Conversely, *vm.swappiness = 0* usually relies on software that does its own caching, like database servers.

Indeed, it’s always a tradeoff since less swapping means more interactivity but worse input-output performance and vice-versa.

### 3.3. Choosing Swappiness

**The value choice for *vm.swappiness* depends on many factors**, mainly having to do with the type of system and its usage:

- virtual machine
- desktop
- web server
- database server
- secondary storage usage
- main memory usage
- amount of RAM

In a way, swappiness decides how much we fill the cache versus the number of swap-outs we perform. **The default swappiness value aims to unburden the system from constant swapping while still enabling the feature to aid our activities**.

In any case, we need hard data to support our choice for *vm.swappiness*.

## 4. Test Swappiness Settings

**While swappiness values should stem from the intended use of a given system, we could perform a general test**:

1. use [*malloc()*](https://www.baeldung.com/cs/memory-allocation#1-malloc) to take up around 90-95% of main memory and hold it
2. start writing about 60% of the data to secondary storage in parallel by, e.g., using [*dd*](https://www.baeldung.com/linux/dd-command) to dump from [*/dev/zero*](https://www.baeldung.com/linux/file-dev-zero-meaning)
3. once ready with the previous step, note down swap usage, page cache usage, and run times
4. reset by killing *malloc()*, removing the *dd* dumps, and [clearing the swap](https://www.baeldung.com/linux/empty-buffer-cache#2-command-to-clear-out-swap)
5. repeat for several trials

By switching up the swappiness value and performing the steps above, we can get an idea of the raw system performance with regard to swap. On the other hand, by changing the test procedures from a pure dump to a complex set of operations, we can gain some insight into our particular system’s behavior in relation to *vm.swappiness*.

## 5. Summary

In this article, we discussed one of the main swap settings – swappiness.

In conclusion, although there is a sane default and we can change it easily, the value of swappiness should be chosen carefully on a per-system basis to avoid adverse effects.",

      "content": "Swappiness is a Linux kernel parameter that controls how aggressively the system moves inactive memory pages from RAM to swap space.

- It represented by a value between 0 and 100.
- A higher value (closer to 100) increases swapping, freeing more RAM but potentially slowing performance due to disk I/O.
- A lower value (closer to 0) reduces swapping, keeping data in physical memory for faster access.
- The default swappiness value is 60 in most Linux distributions.
- Can be adjusted to optimize system performance based on available RAM and workload type.
- Ideal for servers or high-memory systems to lower swappiness, minimizing unnecessary swap usage.

## Displaying the Swappiness Value of the System

Explore the steps to retrieve and display the current swappiness value of a Linux system. Using the  command, you can easily check the active swappiness setting and gain insights into the system’s memory management behavior.

### **Step 1**: Check the Current Swappiness Setting ( sysctl )

- Use the command `sudo sysctl vm.swappiness` to check the current swappiness value.
- The default swappiness value in most Linux distributions is 60.
- This command helps you quickly view and understand how actively your system swaps data between RAM and disk.

**Command:**

`sudo sysctl vm.swappiness`
#### **Output:**

### Step 2: Check the Current Swappiness Setting (Procps)

Use the command `cat /proc/sys/vm/swappiness` to display the current swappiness value.

- The file `/proc/sys/vm/swappiness` holds the kernel parameter that determines how aggressively data is moved from RAM to swap space.
- This command outputs the numeric value representing the system’s active swappiness setting.
- `cat /proc/sys/vm/swappiness` to display the current swappiness value. This file stores the kernel parameter that defines how aggressively data is swapped from RAM to disk. The command outputs the numeric value of the active swappiness setting.

#### **Command:**

cat /proc/sys/vm/swappiness

#### **Output:**

## Changing the Swappiness Value

Here are the steps to change the swappiness value in Linux.

### **Step 1**: Create the Entry of Suitable Value

Open the  file using a text editor to create or modify the swappiness entry.

- Use the command `sudo gedit /etc/sysctl.conf` (or any preferred editor) to access the file.
- Add or update the line `vm.swappiness=<desired_value>` to set your preferred swappiness level.
- If the entry is missing, create it manually to ensure the change is saved.
- This step makes the swappiness configuration persistent across system reboots.
- /etc/sysctl.conf file by using a text editor. Open the file with the command sudo gedit /etc/sysctl.conf and change the value of vm.swappiness to your desired setting. If the entry doesn't exist, create it. This step ensures a persistent adjustment of the swappiness value on your Linux system.

#### **Command:**

`sudo gedit /etc/sysctl.conf`
#### **Output:**

### Step 2: Display the Created Entry

Verify the swappiness entry in the `/etc/sysctl.conf` file using the command `cat /etc/sysctl.conf | grep swappiness`.

- This command displays the file’s contents and filters lines containing the keyword “swappiness.”
- It helps confirm that the swappiness entry has been successfully created or updated in the configuration file.
- /etc/sysctl.conf file by using the command cat /etc/sysctl.conf | grep swappiness. This command displays the content of the file and filters for lines containing "swappiness," confirming the presence of the newly created or modified entry.

#### **Command:**

`cat /etc/sysctl.conf | grep swappiness`
#### **Output:**

### Step 3: Change the Swappiness Value of System

- Change the system’s swappiness value at runtime using the `sysctl` command.
- Run `sudo sysctl vm.swappiness=10` (replace 10 with your preferred value) to apply the new setting instantly.
- This method allows you to test and adjust the swappiness value immediately without rebooting the system.

**Command :**

`sudo sysctl vm.swappiness=10`
